title: API 570 Training in Salt Lake City: Online Piping Exam Prep
description: API 570 exam prep for Salt Lake City piping inspectors: traced waxy crude lines, CUI, dead legs, injection points and truck racks. Self-paced, instructor Q&A.
h1: API 570 Training in Salt Lake City: Self-Paced Exam Prep for Process, Unit and Transfer Piping Inspectors on the Wasatch Front
html:
API 570 exam prep for piping inspectors around Salt Lake City

Measured by length, most of what an inspector looks after at a Salt Lake refinery is pipe: crude lines from the tank farm to the heaters, unit piping through every column and exchanger train, product rundown lines, flare headers and the transfer lines that tie each plant to the pipeline stations around it. The valley's five refineries, in Salt Lake City, North Salt Lake and Woods Cross, also have a piping problem that most Gulf Coast plants do not: a share of their crude is waxy oil from the Uinta Basin that has to be kept warm from the wellhead to the crude unit, so heated, traced and insulated lines run through the offsites.

This page is for piping inspectors, NDT technicians, pipefitters and engineers in the valley who are preparing for API 570. It follows the crude into the refineries, marks where pipeline rules end and API 570 begins, and spends most of its time on the local problems the exam also tests: corrosion under insulation on traced lines, dead legs in a cold winter, injection points and the arithmetic of a circuit's next inspection. There is no Atlantis classroom in Salt Lake City; the course is self-paced on the Atlantis learning portal, with an instructor answering your questions, so it travels with you from unit to unit.

How crude reaches the valley's refineries

Crude arrives in two ways, and both matter to a piping inspector.

By pipeline from Wyoming

The Frontier pipeline, held through Frontier Aspen LLC, runs 289 miles from Casper, Wyoming, to Frontier Station in Utah and, through its connection to the SLC pipeline, supplies Canadian and Rocky Mountain crudes to Salt Lake City area refiners. The 95-mile SLC pipeline carries that crude, along with crude from Wyoming and Utah on connecting systems, into the Salt Lake area. Holly Energy Partners bought the remaining Plains All American interests in both lines in October 2017, making them wholly owned subsidiaries, and HF Sinclair completed its acquisition of Holly Energy Partners in December 2023; HF Sinclair's 2025 annual report lists both pipelines among its midstream assets.

By truck from the Uinta Basin

Utah's Department of Environmental Quality explains that the basin's black and yellow waxy crudes must be heated in the field and hauled in insulated trucks, because they solidify quickly as they cool. Marathon Petroleum describes expanding the waxy crude unloading facility at the terminal beside its Salt Lake City refinery: it now has five lanes instead of two, new skids, meters and pumps, and handles roughly 100 transport trucks a day, with the crude moved by pipe into refinery tankage. Every one of those pumps, meters and lines is piping someone has to inspect, and it carries a product that sets solid if the heat fails.

Where API 570 stops and pipeline rules take over

A Salt Lake piping inspector works next to several cross-country systems that are not API 570 piping:

  • the Frontier and SLC crude lines described above;
  • the UNEV products pipeline, which HF Sinclair's 2025 annual report describes as a 427-mile, 12-inch refined products line running from Woods Cross to Las Vegas and Cedar City, with product terminals near both;
  • the northbound products system of Tesoro Logistics Northwest Pipeline LLC, whose current tariff, published on MPLX's website, runs from Salt Lake Station in Davis County to Burley, Pocatello and Boise in Idaho and Pasco in Washington. When Oil & Gas Journal reported Tesoro's purchase of the system from Chevron in 2012, the sale also included a separate five-mile jet fuel line to Salt Lake City International Airport.

Hazardous liquid pipelines like these are regulated under federal pipeline safety rules at 49 CFR Part 195, which carry their own inspection, integrity management and records requirements. API 570 is written for in-service process piping, and an owner's inspection plan has to say where its piping system ends: at the station block valve, the custody meter or a named flange. On the exam the boundary appears as scope questions, so read the scope section of API 570 closely, including the services API 570 treats as optional, which include water, steam, steam condensate and boiler feed water.

Steam tracing, insulation and CUI on a waxy crude system

Waxy crude makes corrosion under insulation a bigger subject here than the climate alone would suggest. Lines that would be bare elsewhere are traced and insulated so the wax stays fluid, and every tracer is a possible source of water under the jacket. API 570's list of locations susceptible to CUI names steam-traced piping that may experience tracing leaks, especially at tubing fittings beneath the insulation. It also names dead legs and attachments that protrude from insulated piping and run at a different temperature from the active line, and hot carbon steel piping that runs only intermittently.

All three describe ordinary offsite piping in the valley. A waxy crude line that is pumped in batches cycles between warm and cold. A traced spool next to a truck lane takes splash and snowmelt. A drain or a sample connection sticking out of the jacket stays colder than the line it serves. A practical CUI programme here starts with walking the traced systems and recording damaged jacketing, missing caulking and the tell-tale icicles that mark a steam leak in winter, then removing insulation at the worst points. On the exam, expect questions on which locations are most susceptible and why, more than on the screening methods themselves.

Dead legs and freeze points in a Wasatch winter

API 570 asks for dead legs to be identified and inspected because stagnant sections corrode differently from the flowing line. On the Wasatch Front a dead leg has a second failure mode: water that settles in it can freeze. Bypasses that are kept closed, spare pump connections, a capped header end and the low point of an abandoned line all collect water from wet crude or from steam condensate. A split pipe found after a cold snap is a freeze problem, not a corrosion problem, but the cure is the same as for corrosion: remove dead legs that are no longer needed, and where one must stay, put it on the inspection plan with its own condition monitoring location.

Small-bore connections need the same attention. Vents, drains, instrument tubing and thermowell connections on traced lines are the places where tracing is hardest to fit, insulation is most often missing, and vibration from pumps at a busy unloading rack can add fatigue to the list.

Injection points in Salt Lake units

Where wash water, neutralisers or corrosion inhibitors are injected into a process stream, API 570 allows the injection point to be set up as a separate inspection circuit. The code recommends how far that circuit should reach upstream of the nozzle and downstream past the changes in flow direction where the injected fluid mixes in, and its table of maximum inspection intervals gives injection points a thickness interval of their own. Learn those limits from the edition on your exam window's effectivity sheet rather than from a site procedure that may paraphrase an older edition.

In Salt Lake units, the typical candidates are wash water upstream of hydrotreater effluent air coolers and the overhead systems of crude and cracking units, where API RP 571's descriptions of ammonium bisulfide and ammonium chloride corrosion explain why the injected water matters. Neither is on the current API 570 Body of Knowledge, which examines listed RP 571 sections such as sour water corrosion, hydrochloric acid corrosion, sulfidation and corrosion under insulation, but a candidate who has followed an injection circuit on a real unit will find the exam's questions on them much easier.

Worked example: a waxy crude unloading header

This example uses illustrative figures. An NPS 8, Schedule 40 carbon steel header carries heated waxy crude from a truck unloading rack to refinery tankage. The outside diameter is 8.625 inches and the nominal wall is 0.322 inch. The design pressure is 285 psig. Assume an allowable stress S of 20,000 psi, a seamless pipe quality factor E of 1.0, a weld joint strength reduction factor W of 1.0 and a coefficient Y of 0.4.

  1. Pressure design thickness, ASME B31.3: t = P D ÷ [2 (S E W + P Y)] = 285 × 8.625 ÷ [2 × (20,000 + 114)] = 2,458.1 ÷ 40,228 = 0.061 inch.
  2. Required thickness: assume the owner's structural minimum for NPS 8 in this service is 0.120 inch. The required thickness is the larger of the pressure design and structural values, so 0.120 inch governs; API RP 574 explains how owners set structural minimums.
  3. Corrosion rates at the governing CML: 0.318 inch in 2012, 0.287 inch in 2020 and 0.262 inch in 2025. Long-term: (0.318 − 0.262) ÷ 13 = 0.0043 inch per year. Short-term: (0.287 − 0.262) ÷ 5 = 0.0050 inch per year. API 570 asks the inspector to compare the two and choose the rate that best reflects current conditions; with no change in service, the short-term rate, which gives the shorter life, is the prudent choice.
  4. Remaining life: (0.262 − 0.120) ÷ 0.0050 = 28.4 years.
  5. Thickness interval: half the remaining life is 14.2 years. The owner has classed the line Class 2, because the rack is a busy area with trucks and drivers present, and API 570's maximum thickness interval for Class 2 is ten years. The lesser value governs, so the next thickness measurement is due in ten years. The external visual inspection for Class 2 is due every five years.

The lesson for this header is that its thickness interval is not where the risk lies. CML readings track general internal loss at fixed points, while corrosion under insulation from a leaking tracer is local and may sit between them. The five-year external visual, and the CUI follow-up it triggers, is what protects this line in practice.

Routes into API 570 for Salt Lake piping people

API counts experience gained in the last ten years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, and the amount depends on education. The API 570 certification page gives the full rules; the table shows how they map onto common local jobs.

API 570 eligibility routes for common Salt Lake jobs
BackgroundTypical local roleExperience API asks for
Engineering or technology degreeReliability, corrosion or project engineer at a refineryOne year supervising or performing piping inspection
Two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technologyPiping designer, QC technician, contract inspectorTwo years in piping design, construction, repair, operation or inspection, one of them in inspection
High school diploma or equivalentPipefitter, welder, operator, NDT technicianThree years, including one in supervision or performance of inspection
No formal educationLong-serving craft or operations staffFive or more years, including one in inspection

Welders from Salt Lake Community College's Welding Technology programme, which includes a required course in welding inspection and welding metallurgy, and from Davis Technical College's welding programme in Kaysville often move into piping repair and then into QC, which builds the inspection year. UT technicians who run thickness surveys on CML circuits are already doing inspection work; Atlantis's NDT training in Salt Lake City covers the ASNT SNT-TC-1A methods, and the standards summary for API 570 is a useful first read before the full code.

Studying API 570 between unit outages

API 570's open-book half rewards people who know their way around ASME B31.3, which is long and densely cross-referenced. Learn where the pressure design equations, the allowable stress tables, the quality factors and the leak test rules sit, and practise reaching them in the PDF within a minute or two. The Body of Knowledge describes the closed-book half as everyday working knowledge of API 570 and its reference documents, so read API 570, the whole of API RP 574 and the examined sections of API RP 571 until you can answer without looking.

The course is self-paced, so a candidate can push hard in a quiet month and ease off during an outage. A good pattern is to work one practice section on each day off and to bring every piece of piping you inspected that week back to the code: which class is it, which CMLs govern, would it have an injection point circuit? When a B31.3 clause reads two ways, send it to the instructor, who answers from the code text.

Sponsoring a piping inspection group in the valley

A refinery inspection department, a contractor running CML surveys at several Salt Lake plants, or a pipeline company whose staff look after station piping can enrol a group, and fees are quoted on request. Candidates progress at their own pace and ask their own questions, so day and night shifts can prepare for the same exam window without being in the same place. API still assesses each candidate on their own application, and the employer's part is to confirm experience accurately and promptly.

faq.q: Can I take an in-person API 570 preparation class in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: Atlantis does not run one. Its API 570 course is online and self-paced, with an instructor answering questions as you study, so you can prepare in the valley without travelling. The exam is the only part that must be taken in person: API 570 runs at Prometric test centres, and Prometric lists test centres in and around Salt Lake City that you can choose when you schedule.

faq.q: Is the Frontier crude pipeline from Wyoming inspected under API 570?
faq.a: No. Cross-country lines such as the Frontier and SLC crude pipelines, UNEV and the products system that runs north to Idaho and Washington are hazardous liquid pipelines under the federal rules at 49 CFR Part 195. API 570 covers in-service process piping, so its work begins where the operator's inspection plan says the refinery or terminal piping system starts, usually at a defined valve, meter or flange.

faq.q: Are the lines at a refinery truck unloading rack API 570 piping?
faq.a: They are usually within the refinery or terminal owner's piping inspection programme, and API 570 is the code most owners apply to them. The interesting exam questions are about class: crude that does not significantly vaporise can fall into Class 3, but API 570 keeps that class for lines away from high-activity areas, and a busy truck rack is exactly that kind of area.

faq.q: Do steam tracing lines come under API 570?
faq.a: API 570 treats steam and steam condensate services as optional, so the owner decides whether to bring tracing into the programme. Whatever that decision, the tracing matters to the process line it heats, because API 570 lists steam-traced piping with tracing leaks among the locations most susceptible to corrosion under insulation. Inspect the tracer joints and jacketing on the product line even if the tracing itself is outside scope.

faq.q: How many CMLs does API 570 require on a piping circuit?
faq.a: API 570 does not set a fixed number. The inspector selects condition monitoring locations according to the expected damage, the likelihood of localised corrosion and the consequence of a failure, and places more where damage is likely to vary, such as elbows, tees, injection points and dead legs. Exam questions test the reasoning behind CML selection rather than a count.

faq.q: Do I need to know Utah's boiler and pressure vessel rules for the API 570 exam?
faq.a: No. Utah's Rule R616-2, administered by the Labor Commission, covers boilers and pressure vessels and is not part of the API 570 Body of Knowledge. The exam tests API 570, ASME B31.3 and the other publications on the effectivity sheet for your window. Local rules matter at work, not on the exam paper.

faq.q: I run UT thickness surveys at a Woods Cross refinery. Does that count toward API 570?
faq.a: Thickness surveys on piping circuits are inspection work, so they can count, provided your employer was an authorized inspection agency or you worked under contract to one and API can verify the dates and duties. How much you need depends on your education: three years with a high school diploma, two with a two-year technical qualification, one with an engineering degree.

faq.q: Can a Salt Lake contractor enrol its whole CML survey crew?
faq.a: Yes. Inspection contractors and refinery groups can enrol several candidates, and fees are quoted on request. Each person works through the material and practice papers at their own pace and puts their own questions to the instructor, which suits crews spread across different plants and shifts. Each candidate still applies to API and meets the eligibility rules individually.
